title: Red Flags & Common Mistakes
summary: Some answer patterns hurt a candidate regardless of how good the underlying story is. Learn the specific patterns interviewers are trained to flag — badmouthing, over-claiming credit, no real reflection, rambling, and answers with no measurable outcome.

slides.markdown:
So far this group has been about building good stories and scoping them correctly. This topic flips the lens: a set of specific delivery patterns that damage a story regardless of how strong the underlying incident actually is.

These patterns are worth memorizing on their own because interviewers are explicitly trained to notice them — they're not subtle personal taste, they're named failure modes in most interviewer training material. Recognizing them in your own rehearsed answers before the interview is far easier than catching them live.

slides.sectionTitle: Badmouthing a former manager or company
slides.markdown:
Any story where the villain is clearly your former manager, team, or company — described with real negativity rather than neutral facts — reads badly regardless of whether your account is accurate. Interviewers can't verify the details, so they default to judging your framing choice: talking negatively about a past employer to a stranger you're trying to impress suggests you might do the same about this company to your next interviewer.

The fix isn't lying about a bad situation — it's describing it in neutral, factual terms and putting the focus on your own response. "My manager and I had different views on prioritization, so I..." lands very differently from "my manager had no idea what they were doing, so I..." even when both describe the same underlying reality.

slides.sectionTitle: Taking full credit for a team result
slides.markdown:
A story told entirely in "I" language about an outcome that obviously involved a team — a launch, a migration, an incident response — reads as either dishonest or as a sign you don't recognize others' contributions, both bad signals for collaboration-heavy roles.

The fix, covered in more depth in [answering for your level](behavioral-calibrating-level), is precise language: credit the team for what they executed, and be specific about your own distinct contribution — the decision you made, the piece you personally built, the alignment you personally drove. "I decided we needed X, and the team built it" is both more honest and reads better than either extreme of "I did everything" or an evasive "we did it" that hides your actual contribution.

slides.sectionTitle: No real self-reflection in a failure story
slides.markdown:
A failure story that ends at "and then it went wrong" without a clear account of what you personally misjudged and what you changed afterward isn't actually answering the question — the question is testing self-awareness and growth, and a story with no reflection provides neither.

A related, subtler version: a failure story where the failure is entirely attributed to external factors ("the requirements changed," "the other team dropped the ball") with no admission of anything you could have done differently. Even in a genuinely externally-caused failure, a strong answer finds the part that was within your control — how you communicated, what you could have flagged earlier, how you'd change your own process next time.

slides.sectionTitle: Rambling past the point of enough signal
slides.markdown:
Continuing to add detail after the interviewer has clearly gotten what they need — visible in body language, a note being written, or a "got it, let's move on" cue — burns time that could go to a second story, and can undercut an otherwise strong answer by diluting the strongest parts with padding.

A useful discipline: deliver the STAR shape in roughly 90 seconds to 2 minutes for the initial answer, then stop and let the interviewer drive with follow-ups rather than pre-emptively answering questions they haven't asked yet. If they want more depth on a specific part, they'll ask — and that follow-up is often the part of the answer that actually earns the strongest score.

slides.sectionTitle: An answer with no measurable outcome
slides.markdown:
"And it went well" or "and the team was happy with it" as a closing line, with no number or verifiable detail attached, is one of the most common ways an otherwise decent story loses points. Interviewers are trying to write down evidence, and "it went well" gives them nothing to write.

Every story in your bank should end with something concrete: a percentage, a time saved, an incident avoided, an adoption count, or at minimum a specific verifiable detail ("the feature shipped a week ahead of the original date" beats "it shipped on time"). If you genuinely don't have a number for a given story, that's a signal the story needs more prep before the interview, not that the outcome doesn't matter.

slides.sectionTitle: A self-aware vs. a defensive answer to 'tell me about a failure'
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
| | Defensive version | Self-aware version |
|---|---|---|
| Framing | "It wasn't really my fault, the requirements kept changing" | "I should have flagged the requirement churn to my manager sooner instead of absorbing it silently" |
| Detail on the mistake | Vague or absent | Specific: names exactly what was misjudged |
| Emotional tone | Justifying, slightly irritated | Matter-of-fact, no residual defensiveness |
| Follow-through | None mentioned | A specific process change made afterward |

Both candidates might be describing the exact same incident. The self-aware version isn't about being harder on yourself for its own sake — it's about demonstrating you can extract a lesson from a bad outcome, which is the actual thing being tested.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall recap as a pre-loop self-check
slides.markdown:
A five-item check to run against your top stories the night before a loop:

1. Does any story frame a former manager, team, or company negatively rather than neutrally?
2. Does any story use "I" for an outcome that clearly involved a team, with no team credit?
3. Does my failure story include a specific thing I'd have done differently, not just external causes?
4. Can I deliver each story's core in under two minutes without padding?
5. Does every story end with a concrete, verifiable outcome rather than "it went well"?

Running this checklist against a story you thought was strong often surfaces one or two of these patterns hiding in otherwise good material — they're easy to miss in your own head, and easy to catch once you're checking for them explicitly.

slides.sectionTitle: Red flags carry across the whole loop
slides.markdown:
Unlike scope calibration, which is about matching a target level, these patterns are near-universal — a badmouthing answer or a no-outcome answer reads badly at any level, in any round, at any company. That makes this checklist worth running against every story in your bank, not just the ones you plan to lead with.

The next topic shifts from single-answer mistakes to loop-level dynamics: how these same patterns get noticed and compared across a multi-interviewer panel, and what a debrief actually does with that information.
